subject: Banking
title: What Happens in an IPO
description: A quick win: understand What Happens in an IPO.

hook.text: When a private company sells shares to the public for the first time, it is called an IPO.

buildup.text: The company hires investment banks to underwrite the offering.

discovery.text: Underwriting means the bank guarantees it will buy any unsold shares. The bank takes the risk if demand is weak.

twist.text: Banks deliberately underprice most IPOs. The stock pops on day one, making buyers happy.

climax.text: IPO underpricing is a hidden cost to the company. The bank's real clients are investors who get shares at a discount.

punchline.text: The IPO pop is not luck. Banks underprice on purpose.

quiz.question: Why do investment banks often underprice IPOs?
options: To ensure strong demand and please the investor clients who buy shares

details.summary: An initial public offering transforms a private company into a publicly traded one by selling shares to public investors for the first time, with investment banks managing the process of pricing, marketing, and distributing the new shares.
details.whyItMatters: IPOs unlock liquidity for founders and early investors while giving public investors access to high-growth companies. The IPO process determines billions in valuations and shapes which companies define the next economic era.
takeaways: Companies hire investment banks to underwrite and price the offering
The SEC filing process requires detailed financial disclosure
IPO underpricing is common, transferring value from companies to investors

faq.question: Why is the first-day pop bad for the company going public?
faq.answer: If shares jump 30 percent on day one, the company sold its shares too cheaply. That 30 percent gain went to institutional investors who received allocations, not to the company. The company left money on the table that it could have raised.

faq.question: How long does the IPO process take?
faq.answer: Typically 4 to 6 months from selecting underwriters to listing day. The process includes SEC registration, financial audits, roadshow preparation, pricing negotiations, and regulatory review. Complex cases can take significantly longer.
